title: Seven Loans in Tororo: The Weekend Kiva Stopped Asking Permission
dek: In 2005 Matt Flannery and Jessica Jackley stopped waiting for every answer and posted seven Ugandan businesses to a small website without interest.

story.event: Launching a pilot of seven person-to-person loans to entrepreneurs in Tororo, Uganda
story.summary: After months of business planning and legal uncertainty, Matt Flannery and his then wife Jessica (later Jessica Jackley) decided in early 2005 to launch a small pilot of their online lending idea, dropping interest payments after informal talks with the SEC. Moses Onyango, a pastor and Village Enterprise Fund coordinator in Tororo, Uganda, posted seven local entrepreneurs, whose loans of about $3,100 to $3,500 were funded by the couple's wedding invitation list within a weekend in spring 2005. Kiva launched publicly that autumn with about fifty more Tororo borrowers.
paragraphs: Over Christmas 2004, at Matt Flannery's childhood home in Oregon, he and his wife Jessica, now Jessica Jackley, took stock. In 2004 she had worked in East Africa for Village Enterprise Fund, a charity giving small business grants, and in Tororo, Uganda, had stayed with Moses Onyango, a pastor and the charity's local coordinator. On long bus rides there the couple had shaped an idea: let ordinary people lend small sums online to named entrepreneurs. Back in San Francisco, where Matt wrote software for TiVo, months of plans and meetings followed. Asking for permission, he wrote later, had taken a toll.

The objections were serious. Geoff Davis, who ran the microfinance accelerator Unitus, warned that tracking $25 loans from one lender to one borrower sounded "hard to scale"; Matt left with a pit in his stomach. Jessica approached more than thirty law firms, and many would not touch the securities questions. There was no funding. Flannery later described the dilemma: "begin and be exposed, or don't begin at all."

They chose to begin, small. Matt cold-called the US Securities and Exchange Commission and spent hours with a special counsel who gave no formal opinion but indicated that loans paying no interest were unlikely to be treated as securities. So lenders would earn nothing. Through early 2005 the couple coded in cafés and doughnut shops while Matt kept his job; he bought the domain for $600 and traded his electric guitar for a logo. Onyango posted seven Tororo entrepreneurs, among them Elizabeth Omalla, a widowed fish seller with seven children.

They emailed about 300 people on their wedding invitation list. All seven loans were funded within a weekend that spring, about $3,500 by Matt's account; Onyango recalled $3,100. Jessica later said that if those businesses had failed, the idea would probably have stopped there. Onyango posted monthly updates, and Omalla repaid her loan. In the autumn Kiva went public with fifty more Tororo borrowers; when a large political blog featured it, about $10,000 arrived in a morning, and Matt quit TiVo the following Monday. By 2009 critics such as David Roodman argued that the one-to-one link Kiva advertised had become partly fictional, and Kiva changed how it described its model.

quote.text: Still a prey to uncertainty, one day I decided to leave Bagdad and to give up everything; the next day I gave up my resolution. I advanced one step and immediately relapsed.
quote.source_title: The Confessions of Al Ghazzali, tr. Claud Field, Project Gutenberg eBook #58977
quote.connection: Ghazali describes months of resolving and unresolving before he left his post in Baghdad. The Flannerys' year of plans and meetings had the same shape, and his account names what such wavering costs: not only time, but the slow loss of the reason you began.

reflection: Notice what made the start possible. The objections were not answered; most of them stayed open. What changed was the size of the first step. The Flannerys shrank it until it fitted what they could do without anyone's permission: seven loans, no interest, a wedding list and a friend in Tororo they trusted.

There may be something in your own work that has stalled at the stage of plans and meetings, waiting for a yes that may not come in the form you expect. Ghazali knew the exhaustion of deciding and undeciding. Sometimes the kinder choice, for you as well as for the work, is a smaller version you can actually begin.
invitation: Name one plan that has been waiting on someone else's approval. Write down the smallest version of it you could try this week without that approval, then decide whether to do it.

The first loans were funded quickly in spring 2005 (Flannery: $3,500 in a weekend in April; Onyango: $3,100; Kiva: first loan funded March 2005)

research_notes: Date and amount of the first loans: Flannery's 2007 essay says the seven were funded in a weekend in April 2005 for $3,500; Kiva's own site says the first loan was funded in March 2005; Onyango told PBS in 2006 the businesses received $3,100. The story says 'that spring' and gives both amounts with who said them, and approx_date is set to 2005. Kiva's site says Elizabeth's loan was $500; Flannery's textbox calls her $500 Kiva loan a 'second loan' (after an earlier VEF grant); the story gives no amount for her loan. Names: Jessica was Jessica Flannery at the time (as PBS and the essay call her) and later Jessica Jackley (TED); the story says so once. The SEC conversation was informal: Flannery stresses nothing the counsel said was a formal opinion, which the story keeps. Moses Onyango is described by Flannery as a pastor in Tororo and by PBS as a long-serving Village Enterprise Fund coordinator; the story gives both. The 'large political blog' is DailyKos, per Flannery. The later criticism is reported by PBS's 2010 update, citing David Roodman (Center for Global Development) and a New York Times report; the story attributes it to critics such as Roodman. The essay PDF (hosted on a University of Wisconsin course reading list) loads but is a PDF, so the source checker cannot read names in it; the RePEc record for the article is https://ideas.repec.org/a/tpr/inntgg/v2y2007i1-2p31-56.html. The TED transcript is cited only for Jessica Jackley's later name and role. Country is the United States, where the decision and the website were made; the borrowers were in Uganda.
